research:
Here is the research brief.

---

RESEARCH BRIEF: Instagram Reel — Laser Hair Removal for Dark Skin
For: Oxyderm Laser Clinic | Hetisha voice | Single Reel, booking CTA

---

FINDING 1: FEAR OF BURNS IS THE PRIMARY CONVERSION BARRIER FOR THIS SEGMENT

The data is unambiguous. Fitzpatrick IV-VI clients (Black, South Asian, Middle Eastern, East African) have a documented reason to distrust laser clinics. National media (ABC News, 2023) reported widespread burns caused by clinics using Alexandrite or IPL devices on darker skin. These clients have either experienced this personally, know someone who has, or searched "laser hair removal burns dark skin" before ever walking into a clinic.

Edmonton competitor scan: Balwin Aesthetics leads locally on dark-skin content. Their positioning is physician-led, Fitzpatrick-specific. Most Edmonton laser clinics post generic "smooth skin" imagery that does nothing to address this fear.

The competitive gap is not in pricing or services. It is in trust-building content that names the fear directly and immediately answers it.

Hook angle: "They burned me at another clinic. Here is why that happened and why it would never happen here."
Or: "If a clinic says laser is safe for all skin tones but uses the same device on everyone, leave."

Why it resonates with Oxyderm's ICA: The South Asian, East African, and West African avatar segments in your ICA are not skeptical of laser in general. They are skeptical of getting it wrong. Naming the burn risk directly, then showing the solution (equipment calibrated for Fitzpatrick V-VI), converts skepticism into trust and positions Hetisha as the practitioner who actually knows their skin.

---

FINDING 2: DEVICE SPECIFICITY IS THE CREDIBILITY SIGNAL THIS AUDIENCE SEARCHES FOR

Clients with darker skin are doing their homework. Terms like "Nd:YAG laser dark skin," "is Alexandrite safe for brown skin," and "laser for Fitzpatrick 5" appear consistently in search data and comment sections on competitor posts. A Reel that explains what device Oxyderm uses and why it is the correct choice for darker skin tones answers the exact question this audience is pre-loading before they book.

Competitor gap: Most Edmonton clinics do not state their device type in social content. They say "advanced technology" and "FDA approved" without specifics. That vagueness actually heightens anxiety in high-melanin clients because they have learned vague = potentially wrong device.

Hook angle: "Not all lasers are the same. This is the one we use for your skin tone and here is exactly why it matters."
Or (Hetisha speaking): "Before I treat anyone with darker skin, I set my laser settings based on their Fitzpatrick type. Here is what that actually means for you."

Why it resonates: Hetisha's 10 years in laser and the clinic's Health Canada-approved, calibrated-for-all-skin-tones equipment is a real differentiator. Saying it on camera, technically but plainly, signals expertise this audience cannot find in most local clinics' feeds.

---

FINDING 3: "PROOF ON SKIN THAT LOOKS LIKE MINE" IS THE HIGHEST-SAVE CONTENT FORMAT IN THIS NICHE

Research from the aesthetic clinic content space (Socialmon, 2026) confirms: save rates on before/after carousels showing Fitzpatrick IV-VI results with matched lighting and real session timelines reach 5-8 percent of reach, far above the platform average of 1-2 percent for service businesses. Fitzpatrick V-VI clients specifically will not be moved by smooth-leg stock photography of light skin. They need to see results on skin with melanin.

For a Reel, the hook is showing the result first (before-and-after in motion), then having Hetisha explain the process. Visual proof leads; education follows.

Hook angle: (opens on before-and-after B-roll of darker skin) "This client came to me after being told laser would not work on her skin. Six sessions later..."

Why it resonates: If Oxyderm has client-consented before/after footage on Fitzpatrick V or VI skin, this is your single most powerful piece of content for this segment. Nothing Hetisha says will carry as much weight as showing the actual result on the actual skin tone.

---

FINDING 4: THE UNPOPULAR OPINION AND MYTH-BUST FORMATS ARE OUTPERFORMING GENERAL EDUCATIONAL CONTENT ON REELS IN 2026

Platform data (UGC Copilot, 2026) shows the "Unpopular Opinion" hook format is projecting 34-42 percent hook retention on Instagram Reels, above the 22-30 percent baseline. In the dark-skin laser space specifically, the myth being busted is entrenched and emotionally charged, which means friction (the viewer stopping to decide whether Hetisha is right or wrong) works in the Reel's favor.

The myth that laser is universally unsafe for dark skin is still widespread enough that correcting it publicly, with confidence and specificity, reads as brave authority rather than promotional content. Competitors who post the correction weakly ("Actually laser CAN work on dark skin, it depends...") leave the claim underconfirmed. A practitioner who states it bluntly and backs it with equipment detail, Fitzpatrick context, and results wins the follow and the DM.

Hook angle: "Laser hair removal is not safe for dark skin. That is not true. And here is exactly why the clinics still saying that are 10 years behind."
Or: "Stop letting outdated information keep you from results your skin is fully capable of achieving."

Why it resonates: This format gives Hetisha visible expertise without needing a sales pitch. The audience shares this type of content in community groups because it corrects a belief that has materially affected people they know.

---

FINDING 5: INGROWN HAIRS AND RAZOR BUMPS ARE THE ENTRY-POINT PAIN, NOT SMOOTH SKIN AS AN ASPIRATIONAL CONCEPT

Pseudofolliculitis barbae (ingrown hairs, razor bumps, post-shave hyperpigmentation) disproportionately affects darker skin tones and is the immediate, physical reason this audience seeks out laser. It is not primarily an "I want smooth skin" motivation. It is an "I am in pain, I have dark spots, and nothing I do works" motivation. Content that opens on this specific experience, rather than the aspirational smooth-skin destination, hits closer to the actual trigger.

Competitor gap: Edmonton laser clinic content overwhelmingly leads with aspirational smooth-skin visuals. The physical pain and skin damage caused by shaving and waxing on coarse dark hair is largely absent from local social content, which means the first clinic to address it directly owns that search and save behavior.

Hook angle: "If shaving or waxing your darker skin is leaving you with bumps, ingrowns, or dark spots, that is not your skin being difficult. That is a reason to stop and let the laser do the work instead."

Why it resonates: This reframes the client's current experience as a solvable clinical problem, not a cosmetic preference. For ICA segments dealing with PCOS, coarse hair, or repeated skin damage from waxing, this is the most personally accurate content they will see in their feed. It calls them in before the word "laser" does any heavy lifting.

---

RECOMMENDATION FOR STEP 2:

Lead with Finding 1 or 4 for the hook (highest retention projection, most emotionally charged). Build the body around Finding 2 (device specificity as trust signal). Use Finding 3 for visuals if client before/after footage on darker skin is available. Close on Finding 5 to make the CTA feel like a relief, not a sale.
